Main-effects D-study approximation

Source: R/api-generalizability.R, R/api-gstudy-entry.R
mfrm_d_study_main_effects.Rd

mfrm_d_study() applies a practical D-study projection to the variance components from mfrm_generalizability(). It answers questions such as "what happens to G and Phi if we use 2, 3, or 4 raters?" without re-fitting the Rasch/MFRM model.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_generalizability'
mfrm_d_study(
  x,
  design_grid = NULL,
  residual_scaling = c("highest_order", "single_condition", "none", "sensitivity"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_fit'
mfrm_d_study(
  x,
  design_grid = NULL,
  object_facet = "Person",
  random_facets = NULL,
  residual_scaling = c("highest_order", "single_condition", "none", "sensitivity"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_d_study'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

x

Output from mfrm_generalizability() or an mfrm_fit. If an mfrm_fit is supplied, mfrm_generalizability() is called first.

design_grid

Data frame or named list giving planned counts for each random measurement facet. Column names may be the facet names themselves (for example Rater) or n_ plus the facet name (for example n_Rater). Supply exactly one count column per facet, with unique names and an unambiguous one-to-one correspondence. Extra columns, duplicate aliases for a facet, or a column serving two facets are refused. Counts must be positive integers. When NULL, one row using the observed number of levels is returned.

residual_scaling

How the collapsed residual variance should be scaled when planned facet counts increase. "highest_order" treats the residual as highest-order person-by-all-conditions/error variance and divides by the product of planned counts. "single_condition" divides by the smallest planned facet count, a sensitivity assumption for variation associated with the least-replicated condition. It is not a confidence bound. "none" leaves the residual unscaled. "sensitivity" returns all three assumptions for each design row.

...

Additional arguments passed to mfrm_generalizability() when x is an mfrm_fit. With an already estimated main-effects G-study or its D-study summary, unused arguments are rejected. In particular, composite weights are unsupported here; they require the score-component route from mfrm_g_study().

object_facet, random_facets

Passed to mfrm_generalizability() when x is an mfrm_fit.

object

A main-effects D-study result.

Value

An object of class mfrm_d_study, a data.frame with one row per design scenario and columns for planned facet counts, variance terms, projected G, projected Phi, interpretation bands, and identification status inherited from mfrm_generalizability(). InputRows, UsedRows, and ExcludedRows describe the source G-study, not the planned D-study sample; GStudyDataSource identifies their scope. The data_usage attribute retains its row accounting, including after subsetting. Older source results without accounting have NA counts; they are not assumed to have used all rows. summary(d) returns the coefficient data frame with these saved attributes, rather than generic per-column descriptive statistics. No intervals or new variance-component estimates are computed. GReason, PhiReason, ObjectVarianceReason, RelativeErrorReason, AbsoluteErrorReason and ResidualDivisorReason explain unavailable quantities; empty strings mean no calculation failure. Reasons distinguish unidentified targets, missing/invalid components, zero total variance and numerical range. Fit cautions remain separate in IdentificationStatus and IdentificationNote. ComponentIdentificationChecked and the component_identification attribute retain the source design check.

Details

The projection uses the variance decomposition already estimated by mfrm_generalizability(). For a random measurement facet j, main-effect variance contributes sigma2_j / n_j to the absolute-error denominator. Under the fitted additive model, residual errors are independent across observations. For a complete future crossing with common facet levels for all persons, their mean has variance sigma2_Residual / prod(n_j). Facet-wide shifts cancel from relative comparisons but enter absolute error as sum(sigma2_j / n_j). This justifies "highest_order" within that model. If omitted interactions actually exist, the fitted residual does not recover their separate variances or correlations; dividing it by the product is then an assumption. "single_condition" and "none" are alternative planning assumptions, not estimates of these correlations, confidence bounds, or a guarantee that the true projection lies between them. The relative-decision denominator uses only this scaled residual term. Missing or invalid required components leave the affected coefficient unavailable; they are not zero variance. These are point projections conditional on estimated components, not uncertainty bounds or automatic recommendations for sample size. Returned G/Phi retain full precision, as do the values used for their reference-status labels. Round only for presentation, after any comparisons.

Error variances are evaluated independently of object variance: they remain available when object variance is zero or missing. Zero object variance with positive error gives a coefficient of zero; zero total variance is undefined. For checked sources, only identified variance sums enter the output. For example, two confounded facet main effects can still contribute their identified sum when their planned counts are equal; unequal counts require the separate, unidentified components. Coefficients use scaled sums to avoid overflow. A coefficient can therefore remain calculable even when its error variance exceeds floating-point range. Such unrepresentable quantities are returned as NA with reasons.

This is a pragmatic D-study planning layer, not a full p x r x i ANOVA decomposition. If person-by-rater or person-by-item interactions are a primary estimand, consider mfrm_g_study() and mfrm_d_study() for one or two common random facets, including Person-by-Task, Person-by-Rater, and Person-by-Rater-by-Task. Those functions also accept a single score and estimate the corresponding interaction components explicitly. Changing residual_scaling here only explores assumptions; it does not estimate the omitted interactions.

Pass the result directly to mfrm_report() for full projection tables and their assumptions. Newly created results retain source variance components, estimation settings and observed facet counts. Reports of older compatible results mark missing source details not_recorded; report creation never reconstructs components or computes confidence intervals.

The G and Phi values returned here belong to the generalizability-theory metric family. They should not be interpreted as coefficient alpha, omega, KR-20, or IRT marginal/separation reliability, even though all of those summaries may be displayed on a 0–1 scale in broader reporting dashboards. They remain on the observed numeric score scale inherited from mfrm_generalizability(), not the fitted MFRM latent scale.

References

Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., & Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The dependability of behavioral measurements: Theory of generalizability for scores and profiles. Wiley.

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0 . This framework does not recover the interaction components omitted by the source main-effects model.

See also

plot.mfrm_d_study(), mfrm_generalizability(), mfrm_d_study(), evaluate_mfrm_design(), recommend_mfrm_design(), plot_data()

Examples

# Saved synthetic JML/RSM analysis of example_core.
# For your own data, fit a model first; see ?fit_mfrm.
example_fit <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "core-jml.rds", package = "mfrmr"))
fit <- example_fit$fit
if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  gt <- mfrm_generalizability(fit)
  ds <- mfrm_d_study(gt, data.frame(Rater = c(2, 3, 4), Criterion = 4))
  ds[, c("n_Rater", "n_Criterion", "G", "Phi",
         "GStatus", "PhiStatus", "IdentificationStatus")]
  # If IdentificationStatus is not "identified", even large G/Phi
  # values remain identification warnings, not decision-ready evidence.
}
#> mfrmr D-study projection
#>   Object of measurement: Person 
#>   Random facets: Rater, Criterion 
#> 
#>   Estimand scale: observed numeric score
#>   G-study rows: 768 input; 768 used; 0 excluded.
#>   Counts start from stored fitted rows; earlier MFRM filtering is not included.
#>   Residual assumption: Divide residual by all facet counts 
#> 
#>  n_Rater n_Criterion         G       Phi
#>        2           4 0.8240540 0.7887498
#>        3           4 0.8753947 0.8447234
#>        4           4 0.9035412 0.8757990
#>   Observed-score planning projections hold estimated variance components fixed.
#>   They do not establish cut-score accuracy or an adequate rating design.
#> 
#>   Note: 0.70 and 0.80 are reference guides, not universal decision rules.
